title: Al-Ghaffar, the Forgiving
hookLine: the Forgiving, again and again, however often you return

cards: The same old thing. A temper that flares at the same person. A habit quit eleven times.
A promise to oneself broken every Tuesday. The first time, asking forgiveness comes easily. By the fifth, it can feel embarrassing.
By the twentieth, a person might stop asking at all, sure there's a limit and sure they've hit it.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told a story about exactly this person: a servant who does the same wrong again and again, and keeps coming back. Bukhari and Muslim both record it, and the answer is a name built for repetition.

teach.b: In the story, a servant sins and says: my Lord, I have sinned, forgive me. And Allah says: My servant knew that he has a Lord who forgives sins and holds to account for them. I have forgiven My servant.
Time passes. The servant does it again, with the same words, and gets the same answer: forgiven. A third time, the same.
Scholars explain the story carefully: it isn't permission to do wrong. It's about the one who keeps sincerely turning back, meaning it each time. For that person, the door doesn't close.

teach.h: GH-F-R — TO COVER, LIKE A HELMET.
teach.b: The root of the name is gh-f-r, to cover. A mighfar is a helmet, the thing that covers the head and protects it in battle.
So forgiveness, maghfirah, is more than a pardon: the wrong is covered over, and you're protected from its harm. Three names of Allah come from this root.
Al-Ghafir, the one who forgives. Al-Ghafur, whose forgiveness is great. And al-Ghaffar, built on a form that means again and again, as often as it's needed: the name for the twentieth time.
The prophet Nuh told his people: ask your Lord for forgiveness; He is ever Ghaffar.
And Bukhari records the Prophet saying that he himself asked Allah's forgiveness more than seventy times a day.
If he did, the fifth time is no reason for embarrassment. Astaghfirullah: I ask Allah's forgiveness. Muslims say it after prayers, at small slips, and in the middle of ordinary days.

how: Muslims say astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness, many times a day: after each prayer (often three times), at small slips, and in longer forms like sayyid al-istighfar, following the Prophet's practice of seeking forgiveness more than seventy times a day.

o: the one who forgets every wrong done
the one who forgives only the first time
the one who forgives again and again

games.q: the family of gh-f-r — tap the pairs.

s: the hadith of the returning servant permits doing wrong
scholars say it's for the one who keeps sincerely turning back.
the Prophet asked forgiveness more than seventy times a day
al-Ghafur and al-Ghaffar come from different roots
both from gh-f-r, to cover; al-Ghaffar stresses again and again.

games.q: the servant sins, asks forgiveness, is forgiven, and does it again. he asks a second time. what happens?
o: he's told he's used up his chance
games.why: forgiven again, and a third time: My servant knew he has a Lord who forgives (Bukhari; Muslim).

practice: Let your same old thing come to mind and look at it honestly, the way you'd look at a scrape on your knee, without flinching or arguing for it, noticing any tiredness or shame.
Then picture it covered, gently, like a helmet over a head or a blanket over someone sleeping, and breathe under that covering.
If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, once, slowly, and mean it, even if you've said it for this a hundred times before.

wordCard.voice: Al-Ghaffar. The Forgiving, again and again: the one who covers wrongs as often as a person sincerely returns. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Forgiving, again and again; from gh-f-r, to cover.

carryVoice: Your line: forgiven again. The twentieth time is what the name is for. That's day two hundred forty-four.
